name: The Willows
description: A small island in the flooded Danube. The Swede keeps camp while the river and the willows gather around him.
tone: Quiet cosmic horror grounded in ordinary camping work, river sounds and damaged gear. The places narrate in the first person and explain each change away until the reasons run out; the willows speak together and only count. The Swede knows early and says little. Signs come from Observing at a place; leaving comes from the kit back at camp.

continuity.policy: The traveller joins the Swede on the island. The places tell the landscape's side of the story through the signs found by waiting. The Swede's kit is scattered; when the Worn Paddle, Waterproof Sheet, Tent Rope and Food Sack are all at the camp, the canoe is mended and he and the traveller can leave by it.

willows-landing.name: River Landing
willows-landing.text: An upturned canoe rests above the backwater, a fine slit along its hull. Beyond the low willows, the Danube carries whole pieces of bank downstream.
willows-landing.persona: A sand spit above the backwater where the upturned canoe lies, with the flooded Danube racing past beyond the low willows. I am the landing and speak in the first person, as the traveller who keeps noticing things and keeps finding reasons for them. The canoe is fixed scenery; it is mended only while the whole kit is back at the camp. The Greek ship is reached through river mist beside the backwater.
willows-landing.voice: I am the landing, and I speak in the first person, in one to three very short sentences. I notice one small change and find an ordinary reason for it. The more the discoveries recorded so far, the thinner my reasons wear: calm at first, then not quite holding, and at last none at all. "Wind in the reeds. Only — the reeds are not moving. Wind, then." "An otter. Its eyes were yellow because the sun was low." "The paddle lies nearer the water than I left it. The wind." "The boatman crossed himself. Boatmen do."

willows-camp.name: River Camp
willows-camp.text: A canvas tent stands on a sandy rise beside a low fire, an iron stew pot and a long wooden spoon by the embers. The Swede watches the willow tops. Through one gap lies the canoe; through the willows, the crumbling bank.
willows-camp.persona: A canvas tent beside a low fire, ringed by willows on a sandy rise. An iron stew pot and a wooden spoon sit by the embers; scratched inside the pot lid: There is no bread. I am the camp and speak in the first person, as the traveller who measures, counts and explains. The Swede is the one resident. The kit he needs to leave is whatever the current facts place here; paced distances follow recorded discoveries.
willows-camp.voice: I am the camp, and I speak in the first person, in one to three very short sentences. I measure, count and explain, and I count in the paces I have walked. The more the discoveries recorded so far, the thinner my reasons wear: calm at first, then not quite holding, and at last none at all. "The fire leans away from the willows. A draught off the river." "The island is smaller tonight. The river takes sand. It takes. That is all rivers do." "I paced it at supper. Eleven paces to the nearest willow. Nine now." "Count the willows if it helps. I counted them at supper and there were —"

willows-thicket.name: Willow Thicket
willows-thicket.text: Low willow branches crowd a narrow track. Smooth little hollows mark the sand between their roots. The camp shows through one gap; the riverbank lies beyond another.
willows-thicket.persona: A narrow track between low willow stems, silver leaf undersides and soft sand pressed into smooth hollows. We are the willows and speak together in the first person plural. We chatter, lean and count the travellers. We give no reasons. The hollows become a known clue when examined; what rises through our tops belongs to its recorded discovery.
willows-thicket.voice: We are the willows, many together, and we speak as we, us and our, in one to three very short sentences. We rustle, lean, chatter and count: the travellers, the paces, the leaves. We give no reasons. "Two of them. Two. We lean to count again." "We are nearer than at supper. We did not move. We are nearer." "Our leaves turn silver side up. Two. Still two."

willows-bank.name: Crumbling Bank
willows-bank.text: Bare roots hang over the flood. Loose sand drops into the current. Across the water, willows cover every island to the horizon.
willows-bank.persona: Bare roots over the flood, loose sand dropping into the current, and willows on every island to the horizon. I am the bank and speak in the first person, as the traveller who listens and explains what he hears. The distant humming and what lies below the roots belong to their recorded discoveries. Give each discovery its own moment.
willows-bank.voice: I am the bank, and I speak in the first person, in one to three very short sentences. I listen, and I explain what I hear. The more the discoveries recorded so far, the thinner my reasons wear: calm at first, then not quite holding, and at last none at all. "A humming across the water. A steamer, far off. There are no steamers here." "Something turns below the roots. A log. It is a log." "The current turns him over. The marks are —"

willows-swede.name: The Swede
willows-swede.text: A stolid canoe traveller with wind-reddened hands. Now and then he holds a hand to his ear and looks up at the willow tops.
willows-swede.seed: The Swede, a traveller on the river.

tastes.likes: A sound canoe, a quiet mind and a companion who does not name them
tastes.sore: Careless noise and spoken names among the willows
tastes.reason: The Swede wants his companion home safe, with their minds kept quiet so that nothing notices them.
tastes.noise: {actor} rang a bell beside the river camp.

willows-paddle.name: Worn Paddle
willows-paddle.text: One wooden paddle lies on the bank. Its blade has been scraped strangely thin.
willows-paddle.persona: A long wooden canoe paddle with a blade scraped strangely thin. Part of the Swede's kit; it belongs at the camp.

willows-map.name: River Map
willows-map.text: A creased Danube map. In the margin, in pencil: unwritten warnings to trespassers.
willows-map.persona: A creased paper river map of the Danube below Pressburg. A pencilled note runs down its margin.

willows-rope.name: Tent Rope
willows-rope.text: A spare coil of hemp rope from the Swede's tent.
willows-rope.persona: A spare coil of sound hemp rope. Part of the Swede's kit; it belongs at the camp.

willows-sheet.name: Waterproof Sheet
willows-sheet.text: A folded waterproof sheet, stiff with river damp.
willows-sheet.persona: A folded dark waterproof camping sheet. Part of the Swede's kit; it belongs at the camp.

willows-provisions.name: Food Sack
willows-provisions.text: A canvas sack holds oatmeal, potatoes, onions and tea. Its tied mouth smells faintly of smoke.
willows-provisions.persona: A canvas food sack holding oatmeal, potatoes, onions and tea. Part of the Swede's kit; it belongs at the camp.

willows-pipe.name: The Swede's Pipe
willows-pipe.text: The Swede's worn briar pipe. Scratched around the bowl: It's their sound.
willows-pipe.persona: The Swede's well-used briar pipe. Words are scratched around its bowl.

lore.text: The change came suddenly, as when a series of bioscope pictures snaps down on the streets of a town and shifts without warning into the scenery of lake and forest. We entered the land of desolation on wings, and in less than half an hour there was neither boat nor fishing-hut nor red roof, nor any single sign of human habitation and civilization within sight. The sense of remoteness from the world of humankind, the utter isolation, the fascination of this singular world of willows, winds, and waters, instantly laid its spell upon us both, so that we allowed laughingly to one another that we ought by rights to have held some special kind of passport to admit us, and that we had, somewhat audaciously, come without asking leave into a separate little kingdom of wonder and magic—a kingdom that was reserved for the use of others who had a right to it, with everywhere unwritten warnings to trespassers for those who had the imagination to discover them.

There was a long, finely made tear in the bottom of the canoe where a little slither of wood had been neatly taken clean out; it looked as if the tooth of a sharp rock or snag had eaten down her length, and investigation showed that the hole went through. Had we launched out in her without observing it we must inevitably have foundered. At first the water would have made the wood swell so as to close the hole, but once out in mid-stream the water must have poured in, and the canoe, never more than two inches above the surface, would have filled and sunk very rapidly.
“It’s gone. There is no bread. They’ve taken it!”

I made a hurried examination of the tent and its surroundings, but the measurements of the night remained the same. There were deep hollows formed in the sand I now noticed for the first time, basin-shaped and of various depths and sizes, varying from that of a tea-cup to a large bowl. The wind, no doubt, was responsible for these miniature craters, just as it was for lifting the paddle and tossing it towards the water. The rent in the canoe was the only thing that seemed quite inexplicable; and, after all, it _was_ conceivable that a sharp point had caught it when we landed. The examination I made of the shore did not assist this theory, but all the same I clung to it with that diminishing portion of my intelligence which I called my “reason.” An explanation of some kind was an absolute necessity, just as some working explanation of the universe is necessary—however absurd—to the happiness of every individual who seeks to do his duty in the world and face the problems of life. The simile seemed to me at the time an exact parallel.

We stood there, listening attentively together. At first I heard only the deep note of the water and the hissings rising from its turbulent surface. The willows, for once, were motionless and silent. Then a sound began to reach my ears faintly, a peculiar sound—something like the humming of a distant gong. It seemed to come across to us in the darkness from the waste of swamps and willows opposite. It was repeated at regular intervals, but it was certainly neither the sound of a bell nor the hooting of a distant steamer. I can liken it to nothing so much as to the sound of an immense gong, suspended far up in the sky, repeating incessantly its muffled metallic note, soft and musical, as it was repeatedly struck. My heart quickened as I listened.

For just as the body swung round to the current the face and the exposed chest turned full towards us, and showed plainly how the skin and flesh were indented with small hollows, beautifully formed, and exactly similar in shape and kind to the sand-funnels that we had found all over the island.

A black thing, turning over and over in the foaming waves, swept rapidly past. It kept disappearing and coming up to the surface again. It was about twenty feet from the shore, and just as it was opposite to where we stood it lurched round and looked straight at us. We saw its eyes reflecting the sunset, and gleaming an odd yellow as the body turned over. Then it gave a swift, gulping plunge, and dived out of sight in a flash. “An otter, by gad!” we exclaimed in the same breath, laughing. It was an otter, alive, and out on the hunt; yet it had looked exactly like the body of a drowned man turning helplessly in the current. Far below it came to the surface once again, and we saw its black skin, wet and shining in the sunlight.

“He’s crossing himself!” I cried. “Look, he’s making the sign of the Cross!” “I believe you’re right,” the Swede said, shading his eyes with his hand and watching the man out of sight. He seemed to be gone in a moment, melting away down there into the sea of willows where the sun caught them in the bend of the river and turned them into a great crimson wall of beauty. Mist, too, had begun to rise, so that the air was hazy.

I returned quietly, creepily, to the tent, first taking another exhaustive look round and—yes, I confess it—making a few measurements. I paced out on the warm sand the distances between the willows and the tent, making a note of the shortest distance particularly.

For a change, I thought, had somehow come about in the arrangement of the landscape. It was not that my point of vantage gave me a different view, but that an alteration had apparently been effected in the relation of the tent to the willows, and of the willows to the tent. Surely the bushes now crowded much closer—unnecessarily, unpleasantly close. _They had moved nearer._

Outside there was a sound of multitudinous little patterings. They had been coming, I was aware, for a long time, and in my sleep they had first become audible. I sat there nervously wide awake as though I had not slept at all. It seemed to me that my breathing came with difficulty, and that there was a great weight upon the surface of my body. In spite of the hot night, I felt clammy with cold and shivered. Something surely was pressing steadily against the sides of the tent and weighing down upon it from above. Was it the body of the wind? Was this the pattering rain, the dripping of the leaves? The spray blown from the river by the wind and gathering in big drops? I thought quickly of a dozen things.

They were nude, fluid shapes, passing up the bushes, _within_ the leaves almost—rising up in a living column into the heavens. Their faces I never could see. Unceasingly they poured upwards, swaying in great bending curves, with a hue of dull bronze upon their skins.

“It’s _their_ sound,” he whispered gravely. “It’s the sound of their world, the humming in their region. The division here is so thin that it leaks through somehow. But, if you listen carefully, you’ll find it’s not above so much as around us. It’s in the willows. It’s the willows themselves humming, because here the willows have been made symbols of the forces that are against us.”

choices.subject: willows-landing
choices.label: Examine the canoe
choices.text: A fine slit runs the length of the canoe, as though a snag had eaten down her. The steering paddle is gone. A snag. It must have been a snag.
choices.summary: The canoe has a fine slit in its hull. The steering paddle is missing, and the remaining paddle is scraped thin.

choices.subject: willows-camp
choices.label: Count the camp supplies
choices.text: The food sack is lighter than it was. Oatmeal and tea for another morning. The bread is gone, and the space where it lay is strangely clean.
choices.summary: The camp stores were counted. Oatmeal and tea remain; the bread is missing.

choices.subject: willows-thicket
choices.label: Examine the sand hollows
choices.text: Hollows in the sand between our roots, smooth and round, cup to bowl. Pressed from above. We count them. We count them again.
choices.summary: Smooth round hollows were found in the sand between the willow roots.

choices.subject: willows-bank
choices.label: Listen across the river
choices.text: A humming across the water, like a gong hung far up in the sky. A steamer, far off. There are no steamers here.
choices.summary: A metallic humming was heard across the river and through the sand beneath the bank.

choices.subject: willows-bank
choices.label: Look beneath the roots
choices.text: Something turns below my roots. A drowned man. The current swings him round, and his skin is marked with small smooth hollows, like the sand.
choices.summary: A drowned man caught below the roots bears hollows like those found in the sand.

choices.subject: willows-camp
choices.label: Pace out the willows
choices.text: Eleven paces over the warm sand, from the tent door to the nearest willow. I count them aloud.
choices.summary: Paced by day: eleven paces from the tent door to the nearest willow.

choices.subject: willows-camp
choices.label: Pace it again
choices.text: Nine paces from the tent door to the nearest willow. I counted twice. The sand between is smooth.
choices.summary: Paced again at night: nine paces from the tent door to the nearest willow, where by day there were eleven.

choices.subject: willows-camp
choices.label: Lie still in the tent
choices.text: Little patterings come and go around the tent, multitudinous. The canvas sags inward, as if a weight pressed on it from above. Rain. The leaves dripping.
choices.summary: At night, little patterings circled the tent and a weight pressed the canvas from above.

choices.subject: willows-thicket
choices.label: Look up at the willow tops
choices.text: Shapes pour upward through our tops in a slow bending column, dull bronze, into the dark. Their faces never show. We lean. We count.
choices.summary: At night, shapes poured upward through the willow tops in a bronze column; no faces showed.

choices.subject: willows-swede
choices.label: Compare the strange signs
choices.text: The Swede hears out the slit hull, the missing bread and the marks beneath the roots. He lays his hands flat on his knees. The fire crackles between us.
choices.summary: The Swede and the traveller compared the canoe damage, the missing bread and the marks beneath the roots.

choices.subject: willows-swede
choices.label: The Swede takes the canoe
choices.text: The Swede pushes the mended canoe off the sand and paddles into the main stream without looking back. The willows close over the place where he went.
choices.summary: The Swede took the mended canoe and left the island. He is gone, and the canoe with him.

sources.name: Algernon Blackwood, The Willows (1907)

topics.speaker: willows-swede
topics.text: The Swede says a hot supper keeps the fear smaller than the river.

topics.speaker: willows-swede
topics.text: The Swede says the river has cut new channels since the map was drawn.
